1 Introduction to LaMa

Jan-Ole Fischer

Intro_to_LaMa.Rmd

The R package LaMa provides convenient functions for fitting a variety of latent Markov models, including hidden Markov models (HMMs), hidden semi-Markov models (HSMMs), state space models (SSMs) and continuous-time variants via direct numerical maximum likelihood estimation. The core idea underlying this package is given in Mews et al. (2025), namely for all these models the likelihood function has the same structure, and hence unification of inference procedures is attractive.

Model specification in LaMa amounts to defining a custom likelihood function using provided building blocks – similar to stacking Legos. This approach is different (and arguably more difficult) than model specification in packages like moveHMM, momentuHMM, or hmmTMB. The modular approach, however, has the advantage of being more flexible. Specifying simple models is still very easy and convenient while model complexity can be increased to an arbitrary level and arbitrarily fine control is available for advanced users.

In this vignette, we show the simple way: with automatic differentiation (AD), a basic HMM takes only a few lines of code, and the fitted model object gives state decoding, residuals, plots and simulation for free. The vignette Finer control then shows what the convenience functions do, and how to write every part yourself.

Hidden Markov models

We start from the most basic hidden Markov model (HMM). An N-state HMM is a doubly stochastic process in discrete time: observations are generated by one of N possible distributions f_j(x_t), j = 1, \dots, N, and an unobserved N-state Markov chain selects which distribution is active at any given time point. Hence, HMMs are temporally-dependent mixture models, popular in ecology, sports, finance and many other fields (see Zucchini et al. (2016) for a detailed introduction). The two main model assumptions are:

  1. f(s_t \mid s_{t-1}, s_{t-2}, \dots, s_1) = f(s_t \mid s_{t-1}) (Markov assumption)
  2. f(x_t \mid x_1, \dots, x_{t-1}, x_{t+1}, \dots, x_T, s_1, \dots, s_T) = f(x_t \mid s_t) (conditional independence assumption).

The hidden state process is described by an N-state Markov chain which is fully characterised by its initial distribution \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(1)} = (\Pr(S_1 = 1), \dots, \Pr(S_1 = N)) and the one-step transition probabilities \gamma_{ij} = \Pr(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i), \quad i,j = 1, \dotsc, N. These are typically summarised in a transition probability matrix (t.p.m.) \boldsymbol{\Gamma} = (\gamma_{ij})_{i,j = 1, \dots, N}, where row i is the conditional one-step-ahead distribution of the state process given that the current state is i. For example a t.p.m. for a two-state Markov chain could be

library(LaMa)
#> Loading required package: RTMB

(Gamma = matrix(c(0.9, 0.1,
                  0.2, 0.8), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE))
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]  0.9  0.1
#> [2,]  0.2  0.8

We often assume that the Markov chain is stationary, i.e. that it has been running for a long time before our observations started – e.g. when observing an animal’s behavioural states. The initial distribution is then the stationary distribution \boldsymbol{\delta}, which solves \boldsymbol{\delta} \boldsymbol{\Gamma} = \boldsymbol{\delta}, \quad \text{s.t.} \; \sum_{j=1}^N \delta_j = 1, and is computed by stationary():

(delta = stationary(Gamma))
#>        S1        S2 
#> 0.6666667 0.3333333

It can be interpreted as the long-run proportion of time spent in each state. For the state-dependent distributions f_j(x_t), a typical choice is a parametric family like normal or gamma distributions with state-specific means and standard deviations.

As we do not observe the states, the likelihood sums over all possible state sequences. This is done efficiently by the forward algorithm, implemented in forward() (see Finer control for details) – for fitting models, we only need to provide the ingredients.

Automatic differentiation via RTMB

LaMa fits models using automatic differentiation (AD) via the RTMB package (loaded together with LaMa), the R interface to Template Model Builder (TMB, Kristensen et al. 2016). You write the likelihood as plain R code, and RTMB provides fast and exact derivatives (without doing any calculations by hand!). This makes model fitting fast and robust, and even complex models with random effects feasible.

As an example, we analyse the trex data set contained in the package. It contains hourly step lengths of a Tyrannosaurus rex, living 66 million years ago, and we aim to understand its behavioural process using HMMs.

head(trex, 5)
#>   tod      step     angle state
#> 1   9 0.3252437        NA     1
#> 2  10 0.2458265  2.234562     1
#> 3  11 0.2173252 -2.262418     1
#> 4  12 0.5114665 -2.958732     1
#> 5  13 0.3828494  1.811840     1

The workflow is always the same. We

  1. define the negative log-likelihood function,
  2. turn it into an AD objective function, and
  3. fit the model by numerical optimisation of the latter.

We fit a stationary 2-state HMM with state-dependent gamma distributions for the step lengths. First, we define a list par of initial parameter values on an unconstrained (real-valued) scale, and a list dat with the data and other fixed quantities. The number of states follows from the parameters, here two means and standard deviations.

par = list(
  log_mu = log(c(0.3, 1)),      # initial means for step length (log-transformed)
  log_sigma = log(c(0.2, 0.7)), # initial sds for step length (log-transformed)
  eta = rep(-2, 2)              # initial t.p.m. parameters (on logit scale)
  )

dat = list(
  step = trex$step   # hourly step lengths
  )

Because par is a named list, we can access parameters by name. The likelihood consists of three building blocks: tpm() computes the transition probability matrix from unconstrained parameters, statedens() computes the density of each observation in each state (the allprobs matrix, with missing observations handled automatically), and forward() computes the log-likelihood from these two, here with the stationary distribution of Gamma as initial distribution.

nll = function(par) {
  getAll(par, dat) # makes everything contained available without $
  Gamma = tpm(eta) # computes transition probability matrix from unconstrained eta
  # Parameter transformations for strictly positive parameters
  mu = exp(log_mu); REPORT(mu)
  sigma = exp(log_sigma); REPORT(sigma)
  # State-dependent densities of all observations
  allprobs = statedens(step, dgamma2, mu, sigma)
  -forward("stationary", Gamma, allprobs) # forward algorithm, stationary initial distribution
}

Three things differ from an ordinary R function:

  • Only parameters are passed. nll takes par as its only argument, and getAll(par, dat) makes all parameters and data available by name. dat is read when MakeADFun() is called, so changes to dat after that have no effect.
  • Parameters are unconstrained. Everything in par lives on the real line and is transformed inside the likelihood, e.g. with exp() for positive parameters. tpm() does this for the transition probabilities.
  • REPORT() keeps results. Reported quantities are available after fitting, so we never have to back-transform parameters by hand.

Next, MakeADFun() turns nll into an AD objective function obj, which contains the objective function fn and its gradient gr, among others. Calling them without arguments evaluates them at the initial parameters:

obj = MakeADFun(nll, par, silent = TRUE) # silent = TRUE suppresses printing
obj$fn()
#> [1] 16378.66
obj$gr()
#>          [,1]     [,2]    [,3]      [,4]     [,5]      [,6]
#> [1,] 609.4426 -2272.55 94.1283 -12144.32 151.3179 -181.5449

We fit the model with nlminb(), providing the gradient. We do not supply the Hessian, as a quasi-Newton method that uses gradients only is typically much faster.

opt = nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr) # minimisation

lama() then runs the reporting at the estimated parameters and returns a model object. Printing it gives a short overview, while summary() shows the estimated state process (transition probability matrix, stationary distribution and mean dwell times) and all reported quantities:

mod = lama(obj)
mod
#> Latent Markov model with 2 states (discrete time, homogeneous)
#> 9999 observations (1 missing), 6 parameters
#> Log-likelihood: -10847.12   AIC: 21706.25   BIC: 21749.51
#> Reported: mu, sigma, delta, Gamma, allprobs
summary(mod)
#> Latent Markov model with 2 states (discrete time, homogeneous)
#> 9999 observations (1 missing), 6 parameters
#> 
#> Transition probability matrix:
#>        S1     S2
#> S1 0.8270 0.1730
#> S2 0.1608 0.8392
#> 
#> Stationary distribution:
#>     S1     S2 
#> 0.4817 0.5183 
#> 
#> Mean dwell times:
#>    S1    S2 
#> 5.779 6.217 
#> 
#> Reported quantities:
#>           S1    S2
#> mu    0.3035 2.506
#> sigma 0.2015 1.491
#> 
#> Log-likelihood: -10847.12   AIC: 21706.25   BIC: 21749.51
#> Maximum gradient component: 0.0141

All reported quantities are elements of mod. Besides our own REPORT()s, forward() always reports delta, Gamma and allprobs. AIC() and BIC() work as for other models:

mod$Gamma # estimated t.p.m.
#>           S1        S2
#> S1 0.8269542 0.1730458
#> S2 0.1608473 0.8391527
mod$mu    # estimated state-dependent means
#> [1] 0.3034935 2.5057090
AIC(mod)
#> [1] 21706.25

Working with the fitted model

The model object contains everything needed for downstream tasks. We can decode the most probable state sequence with viterbi() and plot the decoded time series

mod$states = viterbi(mod)

# defining color vector
color = LaMaColors(2)

plot(trex$step[1:200], type = "h", xlab = "time", ylab = "step length",
     col = color[mod$states[1:200]], bty = "n")
legend("topright", col = color, lwd = 1, legend = c("state 1", "state 2"), bty = "n")

or get the local state probabilities with stateprobs(mod).

As statedens() records the data, densities and parameters, the estimated state-dependent distributions can be plotted directly from the model object, weighted by the local state probabilities:

plot(mod, type = "statedens")

We can do some model checking using pseudo-residuals, which should be standard normally distributed if the model is correct. pseudo_res(mod) computes them from the model object alone, and plot(mod) plots them directly (with one row per data stream):

plot(mod)

Finally, simulate() simulates states and observations from the fitted model, e.g. to check whether it reproduces features of the data, or for simulation studies:

sim = simulate(mod)
head(sim)
#>   state     step
#> 1     2 2.827231
#> 2     2 1.838420
#> 3     2 1.242336
#> 4     2 3.102050
#> 5     2 2.325925
#> 6     2 3.812471

Continue reading with Finer control to see what the convenience functions do and how to write every part yourself, or go straight to Extensions.

Mews, Sina, Jan-Ole Koslik, and Roland Langrock. 2025. “How to Build Your Latent Markov Model: The Role of Time and Space.” Statistical Modelling 25 (6). https://doi.org/10.1177/1471082X251355681.
Zucchini, Walter, Iain L. MacDonald, and Roland Langrock. 2016. Hidden Markov Models for Time Series: An Introduction Using R. Boca Raton: Chapman & Hall/CRC.
